response.question: I've rented a commercial shop in Bengaluru under a written lease for five years. After just one year, the landlord sent me a notice asking me to leave, even though I haven't violated any terms. Can he terminate my lease before the agreed period?
response.answer:
Not necessarily. A notice alone does not settle whether your five-year lease has ended early. That depends on the lease terms, whether it was registered, the reason given in the notice and other relevant circumstances.

Generally, if you pay the rent and comply with your obligations, the landlord is deemed to promise that you may occupy the shop without interruption for the lease period, unless the contract or local usage says otherwise. A lease can also end early in certain circumstances, such as when an agreed event occurs or a valid notice to end it expires.

Check whether your lease gives the landlord an early termination option. If it says the lease can end early but does not say who has that option, the option belongs to the tenant, not the landlord. A lease for more than one year can be made only by a registered document, so it matters whether yours was registered.

The general month-to-month and notice rules apply in the absence of a contract or local law or usage to the contrary. Do not assume that a 15-day notice automatically ends your five-year lease.

The available Central Act text is consolidated, but its exact update date is unknown. The sources do not provide Bengaluru-specific rent law, so a local lawyer should check whether other rules affect your situation.

response.question: I paid the full amount for a property in Kolkata and signed an agreement with the seller. Now the seller is refusing to complete the sale and says he wants to sell the property to somebody else for a higher price. What legal options do I have?
response.answer:
You can discuss a court case for **specific performance** with a property lawyer: this means asking the court to require the seller to complete the agreed sale. In an appropriate case, you can also ask for possession. The court decides what relief to grant. [specific_relief_act_1963:22]

The sale agreement alone does not make you the owner or itself create a right over the property. Generally, for tangible property worth ₹100 or more, ownership is transferred by a registered document. [transfer_of_property_act_1882:54]

Subject to any contrary contract, the seller must sign a proper transfer document when the price has been paid or offered and the buyer presents the document for signing at a proper time and place. [transfer_of_property_act_1882:55]

You may also have a **charge** over the seller’s interest in the property for money properly paid before delivery, plus interest. A charge is a security right over the property; it is not the same as ownership. This applies only if you have not improperly refused to accept delivery. [transfer_of_property_act_1882:55]

In a specific-performance case, you may specifically claim possession and, if that claim is refused, any other relief you are entitled to, including refund of earnest money or a deposit. Ask your lawyer about recovery of the full amount you paid and what can be done urgently about the proposed sale to someone else. [specific_relief_act_1963:22]

The available consolidated text of the Transfer of Property Act has no stated 'as on' date. A lawyer should check the current law and any applicable local provisions.

response.question: I rented a flat in Mumbai for three years, but my landlord and I only signed a normal agreement on stamp paper. We never registered it. Is this agreement legally valid, and can either of us rely on it in court?
response.answer:
Under the available central-law sources, a lease for more than one year can be made only by a registered document. Signing an agreement on stamp paper does not by itself meet that registration requirement. So your unregistered agreement cannot by itself create the intended three-year lease. [transfer_of_property_act_1882:107]

In court, an unregistered document that required registration generally cannot be received as evidence of the property transaction. But it may be received for limited purposes, including a claim asking the court to order performance of a contract, or to prove a separate, incidental transaction that did not require a registered document. Whether either exception applies depends on the issue and is for the court to decide. [registration_act_1908:49]

This does not, by itself, settle every question about your landlord–tenant relationship or either party’s rights. The available sources do not include Maharashtra-specific rules, and the exact consolidation dates of the central Acts provided are unknown.

response.question: My landlord in Delhi cut off my water and electricity to force me to leave the flat. Is he allowed to do that?
response.answer:
If the Delhi Rent Control Act applies to your flat, your landlord cannot cut off water or electricity you enjoy as a tenant without a just and sufficient reason. Both are essential services under the Act.

You can apply to the Rent Controller, the authority that handles these matters. If the Controller is satisfied that the landlord cut the services to force you to leave, the Controller may order their immediate restoration while the matter is being examined. The Controller can make this temporary order without first notifying the landlord. After an inquiry, if the Controller finds there was no just and sufficient reason, the Controller must order the services restored.

The Act does not cover every area or every flat in Delhi. Its application to your flat needs to be checked. If it does not apply, these sources do not establish what remedy is available to you.

response.question: I rent a room month to month with no written agreement. How much notice does my landlord have to give me before asking me to leave?
response.answer:
Usually, for a month-to-month residential lease, the landlord must give 15 days’ notice to end the lease. The 15 days run from when you receive the notice. This default rule applies unless a contract, local law or local usage says otherwise. [transfer_of_property_act_1882:106]

The notice must be in writing and signed by or for the landlord. The law also specifies how it must be delivered. A notice that gives less than 15 days is not automatically invalid if a case is filed after the required period has expired. [transfer_of_property_act_1882:106]

Notice to end a lease is different from an eviction order. For example, if your room is covered by Delhi’s rent control law, the Rent Controller may order possession only on specified grounds. That law applies only in covered Delhi areas and excludes some premises. Your location and circumstances matter. [delhi_rent_control_act_1958:14] [delhi_rent_control_act_1958:3]

response.question: The owner of the house I am renting has sold it to someone else. Does my rental agreement continue with the new owner?
response.answer:
Generally, yes. If your rental agreement is a lease, the sale alone does not normally end it. Unless there is a contract saying otherwise, the new owner takes over the former owner’s rights under the lease while they own the property. If you choose to treat the new owner as responsible for the former owner’s obligations under the lease, those obligations also pass to the new owner. [transfer_of_property_act_1882:109]

The former owner does not stop being responsible for their lease obligations merely because of the sale, unless you choose to treat the new owner as responsible instead. [transfer_of_property_act_1882:109]

The new owner is not entitled to rent arrears that became due before the transfer. If you paid the former owner without reason to believe the transfer had happened, you do not have to pay that same rent again to the new owner. [transfer_of_property_act_1882:109]

Your agreement’s terms and whether the lease has already ended matter. For example, a lease can end when its agreed term expires. [transfer_of_property_act_1882:111]

The available text of the central Act is consolidated, but its exact update date is unknown. State-specific rules may also matter.

response.question: My lease ended last year but I kept living in the flat and the landlord kept accepting my rent every month. Am I still a legal tenant?
response.answer:
Possibly yes. Based on what you describe, you may still be a tenant under a renewed lease. When a tenant stays after a lease ends and the landlord accepts rent, the lease is generally renewed unless there is an agreement to the contrary. This is called “holding over” [transfer_of_property_act_1882:116].

The renewed lease may run month to month or year to year, depending on the purpose for which the property was leased. The fact that you pay monthly does not by itself settle that question [transfer_of_property_act_1882:116]. Your lease terms and any later agreement matter, so your status cannot be confirmed from these facts alone.

response.question: I bought a flat and paid in full, but the seller still has not handed over the original title documents. What is the seller legally required to do?
response.answer:
Generally, because you have paid the full purchase price, the seller must hand over the property’s title documents that are in the seller’s possession or control. These are documents relating to ownership of the property. This rule applies unless your contract provides otherwise. [transfer_of_property_act_1882:55]

There are exceptions if the same documents cover other property: if the seller keeps part of that property, the seller may keep the documents; if all of it is sold to different buyers, the buyer of the most valuable lot may keep them. In either case, on a reasonable request, the person keeping them must produce them and provide true copies or extracts at the requesting buyer’s cost. They must also keep them safe, subject to the exception in the source. [transfer_of_property_act_1882:55]

The available Act text is consolidated, but its exact update date is unknown.
